name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Element existing in liquid state for high temperature

questiontext.text: The element which exists in liquid state for a wide range of temperature and can be used for measuring high temperature is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Among Group 13 elements, melting point generally decreases down the group with a notable anomaly at gallium due to its unusual crystal structure consisting of discrete \(\mathrm{Ga}_2\) molecules.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga}\)) has a very low melting point of about \(303\text{ K}\) (\(29.8\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), so it can exist in the liquid state during summer, while its boiling point is extraordinarily high at \(2676\text{ K}\). Boron has a very high melting point, and aluminium and indium have significantly higher melting points than gallium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because gallium remains liquid over an exceptionally wide temperature range (\(303\text{ K}\) to \(2676\text{ K}\)), it is used in high-temperature thermometry. Therefore, the correct element is \(\mathrm{Ga}\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Identifying a Lewis acid among metal chlorides

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the Lewis concept, a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. Covalent halides with an incomplete octet around the central atom have a vacant orbital and can accept a lone pair of electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\), aluminium has only three valence electrons and forms three covalent bonds with chlorine, leaving only \(6\) electrons in its valence shell (an incomplete octet). In contrast, \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\), \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\), and \(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\) are predominantly ionic halides of Group 2 elements in which the metal cations have a stable noble-gas octet configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because aluminium in \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) is electron-deficient and readily accepts an electron pair to complete its octet, \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) acts as a Lewis acid.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Hybridisation and geometry of tetrahydroxo complex species

questiontext.text: The geometry of a complex species can be understood from the knowledge of type of hybridisation of orbitals of central atom. The hybridisation of orbitals of central atom in \(\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_{4}\right]^{-}\) and the geometry of the complex are respectively

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The geometry of a main-group complex with four monodentate ligands and no lone pairs on the central atom is determined by its steric number, which equals the number of \(\sigma\)-bonds formed around the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the given tetrahydroxo complex species, the central atom is surrounded by four \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ligands forming four \(\sigma\)-bonds and has no lone pairs of electrons. A steric number of \(4\) corresponds to the mixing of one \(s\) orbital and three \(p\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3\) hybridisation. Four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals orient symmetrically in three-dimensional space at bond angles of \(109.5^\circ\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hybridisation of the central atom is \(sp^3\) and the geometry of the complex is tetrahedral.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Acidic nature of Group 13 oxides

questiontext.text: Which of the following oxides is acidic in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group 13, metallic character increases down the group from boron to thallium. Consequently, the nature of the trioxides changes from acidic to amphoteric and then to basic down the group.

Step 2: Evaluation
Boron is a non-metal, so boron trioxide (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is purely acidic and reacts with basic oxides or alkalies to form borates. Aluminium oxide (\(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) and gallium oxide (\(\mathrm{Ga}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and bases. Indium oxide (\(\mathrm{In}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is basic in nature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Among the given Group 13 oxides, \(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) is acidic in nature.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Maximum covalency and absence of d-orbitals in boron

questiontext.text: The exhibition of highest co-ordination number depends on the availability of vacant orbitals in the central atom. Which of the following elements is not likely to act as central atom in \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Forming the octahedral complex ion \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\) requires a coordination number of \(6\), which demands \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation and thus the availability of vacant \(d\) orbitals in the valence shell of the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) belongs to the second period (\(n = 2\)), where only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals are available. Because \(2d\) orbitals do not exist, boron cannot expand its octet beyond \(8\) electrons and its maximum covalency is restricted to \(4\) (as in \(\mathrm{BF}_4^-\)). On the other hand, \(\mathrm{Al}\), \(\mathrm{Ga}\), and \(\mathrm{In}\) belong to periods \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\) respectively, and possess vacant \(d\) orbitals in their valence shells, enabling them to form \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\) ions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Due to the non-availability of \(d\) orbitals, boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) cannot act as the central atom in \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Acidic behaviour of boric acid in water

questiontext.text: Boric acid is an acid because its molecule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boric acid, \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3\), is a weak monobasic Lewis acid rather than a protonic (Brønsted–Lowry) acid.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3\), the boron atom has only \(6\) valence electrons and an empty \(2p\) orbital. It does not dissociate to give up a replaceable \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion directly. Instead, in aqueous solution, it accepts an electron pair from a hydroxyl ion (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)) of a water molecule to form the tetrahedral \(\left[\mathrm{B(OH)}_4\right]^-\) ion, thereby releasing a proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)):
\[\mathrm{B(OH)}_3 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \left[\mathrm{B(OH)}_4\right]^- + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Boric acid behaves as an acid because its molecule accepts \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) from water, releasing a proton.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Order of catenation in Group 14 elements

questiontext.text: Catenation i.e., linking of similar atoms depends on size and electronic configuration of atoms. The tendency of catenation in Group 14 elements follows the order:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Catenation is the ability of atoms of the same element to link with one another through covalent bonds to form chains and rings. Its extent depends directly on the strength of the \(\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{M}\) single bond.

Step 2: Evaluation
Down Group 14, atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases, causing the \(\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{M}\) bond enthalpy to decrease sharply from carbon to silicon and then more gradually from silicon to germanium and tin (\(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C} = 348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{Si} = 297\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Ge}-\mathrm{Ge} = 260\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Sn}-\mathrm{Sn} = 240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Because the \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\) bond is exceptionally strong, carbon shows far greater catenation than silicon, while germanium and tin have nearly comparable, weak catenation tendencies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tendency of catenation in Group 14 elements follows the order \(\mathrm{C} \gg \mathrm{Si} > \mathrm{Ge} \approx \mathrm{Sn}\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Controlling chain length of silicone polymers

questiontext.text: Silicon has a strong tendency to form polymers like silicones. The chain length of silicone polymer can be controlled by adding

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Linear silicones are formed by the hydrolysis and condensation of dialkyldichlorosilanes (\(\mathrm{R}_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\)), which are bifunctional monomers. To terminate the growing chain and control polymer length, a monofunctional chlorosilane is added.

Step 2: Evaluation
Upon hydrolysis, \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) produces \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\), which contains only one reactive \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group. When \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\) condenses with the terminal \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of a growing silicone chain, it caps the chain end with non-reactive methyl groups, preventing further polymerisation. By contrast, \(\mathrm{Me}_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\) propagates linear chains, \(\mathrm{MeSiCl}_3\) forms cross-linked silicones, and \(\mathrm{Me}_4\mathrm{Si}\) has no hydrolysable chlorine atoms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The chain length of a silicone polymer can be controlled by adding \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Order of first ionisation enthalpy in Group 13

questiontext.text: Ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol}^{-1}\)) for the elements of Group 13 follows the order.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy generally decreases down a group as atomic size increases, but in Group 13 the presence of poorly shielding inner \(d\) and \(f\) electrons causes significant deviations from a smooth decrease.

Step 2: Evaluation
From \(\mathrm{B}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}\), atomic size increases, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1\) decreases. From \(\mathrm{Al}\) to \(\mathrm{Ga}\), the filling of \(3d\) orbitals introduces poor nuclear shielding, increasing the effective nuclear charge and making \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1(\mathrm{Ga}) > \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1(\mathrm{Al})\). From \(\mathrm{Ga}\) to \(\mathrm{In}\), the increase in atomic size outweighs the effect of \(4d\) electrons, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1\) decreases. Finally, from \(\mathrm{In}\) to \(\mathrm{Tl}\), the filling of \(4f\) orbitals causes poor shielding (lanthanoid contraction), sharply raising the effective nuclear charge so that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1(\mathrm{Tl}) > \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_1(\mathrm{In})\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first ionisation enthalpy of Group 13 elements follows the order \(\mathrm{B} > \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ga} > \mathrm{In} < \mathrm{Tl}\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Planar and perpendicular arrangement of atoms in diborane

questiontext.text: In the structure of diborane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)) has a bridged structure in which each boron atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised and bonded to two terminal hydrogen atoms and two bridging hydrogen atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation
The two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms lie in one common plane, forming four regular two-centre two-electron (\(2c\text{--}2e\)) \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds. The remaining two bridging hydrogen atoms lie one above and one below this plane, forming two three-centre two-electron (\(3c\text{--}2e\)) \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B}\) banana bonds in a plane perpendicular to the plane of the boron and terminal hydrogen atoms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In diborane, \(2\) boron atoms and \(4\) terminal hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane and \(2\) bridging hydrogen atoms lie in the perpendicular plane.

answer.text: All hydrogen atoms lie in one plane and boron atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane.
\(2\) boron atoms and \(4\) terminal hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane and \(2\) bridging hydrogen atoms lie in the perpendicular plane.
\(4\) bridging hydrogen atoms and boron atoms lie in one plane and two terminal hydrogen atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane.
All the atoms are in the same plane.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Preparation of diborane and borazine inorganic benzene

questiontext.text: A compound \(\mathrm{X}\), of boron reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) on heating to give another compound \(\mathrm{Y}\) which is called inorganic benzene. The compound \(\mathrm{X}\) can be prepared by treating \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) with Lithium aluminium hydride. The compounds \(\mathrm{X}\) and \(\mathrm{Y}\) are represented by the formulas.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boron trifluoride undergoes hydride reduction with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) to form diborane, which further reacts with ammonia at elevated temperature to yield borazine, commonly known as inorganic benzene.

Step 2: Evaluation
Treating \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\) in diethyl ether produces diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)) as compound \(\mathrm{X}\):
\[4\mathrm{BF}_3 + 3\mathrm{LiAlH}_4 \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6 + 3\mathrm{LiF} + 3\mathrm{AlF}_3\]
Heating diborane with ammonia yields borazine (\(\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6\)) as compound \(\mathrm{Y}\), which has a cyclic hexagonal structure isoelectronic and isostructural with benzene:
\[3\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6 + 6\mathrm{NH}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6 + 12\mathrm{H}_2\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Compounds \(\mathrm{X}\) and \(\mathrm{Y}\) are \(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\) and \(\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6\), respectively.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Element present in piezoelectric quartz

questiontext.text: Quartz is extensively used as a piezoelectric material, it contains

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quartz is a crystalline form of silica (silicon dioxide, \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\)) with a three-dimensional covalent network of \(\mathrm{SiO}_4\) tetrahedra.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because quartz is composed of \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\), its constituent elements are silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)) and oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}\)). It does not contain lead (\(\mathrm{Pb}\)), titanium (\(\mathrm{Ti}\)), or tin (\(\mathrm{Sn}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Quartz contains silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Commonly used reducing agent among chlorides

questiontext.text: The most commonly used reducing agent is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A reducing agent undergoes oxidation by losing electrons to attain a more stable higher oxidation state. In Group 14, the stability of the \(+4\) oxidation state relative to \(+2\) is high for tin (\(\mathrm{Sn}\)), whereas for lead (\(\mathrm{Pb}\)) the \(+2\) state is more stable due to the inert pair effect.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{SnCl}_2\), tin is in the \(+2\) oxidation state and readily loses two electrons to form the more stable \(+4\) oxidation state (\(\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}\)), making \(\mathrm{SnCl}_2\) a strong and widely used reducing agent. In \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) and \(\mathrm{SnCl}_4\), the central atoms are already in their maximum oxidation states (\(+3\) and \(+4\)) and cannot be oxidised further. In \(\mathrm{PbCl}_2\), \(\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}\) is already more stable than \(\mathrm{Pb}^{4+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The most commonly used reducing agent among the given compounds is \(\mathrm{SnCl}_2\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Chemical identity of dry ice

questiontext.text: Dry ice is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dry ice is the common name for solidified carbon dioxide, which sublimes directly from the solid phase to the gas phase at atmospheric pressure without melting into a liquid.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because solid carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)) turns directly into gas upon warming without leaving any wet liquid residue, it is called dry ice and is widely used as a refrigerant. Solid \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\), and solid \(\mathrm{N}_2\) are not known as dry ice.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dry ice is solid \(\mathrm{CO}_2\).

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Periodic groups of oxides present in cement

questiontext.text: Cement, the important building material is a mixture of oxides of several elements. Besides calcium, iron and sulphur, oxides of elements of which of the group (s) are present in the mixture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Portland cement is a complex mixture of calcium silicates and calcium aluminates containing oxides of several main-group and transition elements.

Step 2: Evaluation
The average composition of Portland cement includes \(\mathrm{CaO}\) (\(50\text{--}60\%\)), \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) (\(20\text{--}25\%\)), \(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) (\(5\text{--}10\%\)), \(\mathrm{MgO}\) (\(2\text{--}3\%\)), \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\) (\(1\text{--}2\%\)), and \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) (\(1\text{--}2\%\)). Apart from calcium, iron, and sulphur, cement contains magnesium (Group 2, as \(\mathrm{MgO}\)), aluminium (Group 13, as \(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)), and silicon (Group 14, as \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, oxides of elements belonging to groups \(2\), \(13\), and \(14\) are present in cement.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Reasons for small atomic radius of gallium

questiontext.text: The reason for small radius of \(\mathrm{Ga}\) compared to \(\mathrm{Al}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atomic radius is governed by the balance between the addition of new principal electron shells and the effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gallium (\(Z = 31\)) follows the first \(d\)-block transition series, so it has \(10\) inner \(3d\) electrons in addition to its noble-gas core, whereas aluminium (\(Z = 13\)) has only a noble-gas core. Because \(d\) (and \(f\)) orbitals have diffused shapes and poor screening power, the increased nuclear charge in gallium pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus, resulting in a smaller atomic radius for \(\mathrm{Ga}\) (\(135\text{ pm}\)) than for \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(143\text{ pm}\)). The mere presence of higher orbitals or higher atomic number alone would normally increase atomic radius rather than decrease it.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The smaller radius of \(\mathrm{Ga}\) compared to \(\mathrm{Al}\) is due to the poor screening effect of \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals and the resulting increase in nuclear charge.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Factors responsible for linear shape of carbon dioxide

questiontext.text: The linear shape of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The shape of a molecule is determined by the hybridisation of its central atom and the arrangement of \(\sigma\)-bonds around it, while \(\pi\)-bonds lie in planes perpendicular to the \(\sigma\)-bond axis.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) (\(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\)), the central carbon atom forms two \(\sigma\)-bonds with the two oxygen atoms and has no lone pairs, corresponding to \(sp\) hybridisation with a \(180^\circ\) bond angle (linear geometry). The remaining two unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals of carbon overlap sideways with the \(2p\) orbitals of the two oxygen atoms to form two \(p\pi - p\pi\) bonds, maintaining the linear \(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}\) framework.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The linear shape of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) is due to \(sp\) hybridisation of carbon and \(p\pi - p\pi\) bonding between carbon and oxygen.

answer.text: \(p\pi - p\pi\) bonding between carbon and oxygen

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Role of trimethylchlorosilane in organosilicone polymerisation

questiontext.text: \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) is used during polymerisation of organo silicones because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organosilicone polymers are produced by the condensation polymerisation of silanols derived from chlorosilanes. Monofunctional silanes act as chain-terminating agents.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) gives \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\), which possesses only one reactive hydroxyl group. When it condenses with the terminal \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group of a growing silicone chain, it blocks the end terminal of the silicone polymer because the three methyl groups cannot undergo further condensation. In this way, adding \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) controls the chain length of the organosilicone polymer. It does not act as a catalyst.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) is used during polymerisation because the chain length of organo silicone polymers can be controlled by adding \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) and \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) blocks the end terminal of the silicone polymer.

answer.text: the chain length of organo silicone polymers can be controlled by adding \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\)
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) blocks the end terminal of silicone polymer
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) improves the quality and yield of the polymer
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) acts as a catalyst during polymerisation

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Properties of carbon allotropes fullerenes and graphite

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elemental carbon exists in several allotropic forms, including fullerenes and graphite, each with distinct structures and thermodynamic stabilities.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fullerenes (such as \(\mathrm{C}_{60}\)) are closed, soccer-ball or cage-like molecules in which every carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised and bonded to three other carbons, so they are pure forms of carbon without any dangling bonds. Graphite has a layered \(sp^2\)-hybridised hexagonal sheet structure with delocalised \(\pi\)-electrons, making it the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^\circ = 0\)). Furthermore, because the layers in graphite are held by weak van der Waals forces and slide easily over one another, graphite is soft and slippery—not hard.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that fullerenes are cage-like molecules and graphite is the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon.

answer.text: Graphite is thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon
Graphite is slippery and hard and therefore used as a dry lubricant in machines

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - Structure and bonding in diborane diagram

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct. Answer on the basis of Fig. 11.1.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Diagram and Layout
The diagram shows the structure of diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)) containing two central boron atoms, four terminal hydrogen atoms, and two bridging hydrogen atoms (one above and one below the plane of the boron and terminal hydrogen atoms).

Step 2: Evaluation
The four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are regular two-centre two-electron (\(2c\text{--}2e\)) covalent bonds, and these four terminal hydrogen atoms along with the two boron atoms lie in one plane. The two bridging hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to the terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) plane. Out of the six total bonds in the diborane framework, the two bridging \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron (\(3c\text{--}2e\)) banana bonds, not four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct statements are that the two bridged hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane, two of the six bonds can be described in terms of \(3\)-centre \(2\)-electron bonds, and the four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are two-centre two-electron regular bonds.

answer.text: The two birdged hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane;
Out of six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds two bonds can be described in terms of \(3\) centre \(2\)-electron bonds.
Out of six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds four \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds can be described in terms of \(3\) centre \(2\) electron bonds;
The four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are two centre-two electron regular bonds.

name.text: NEETUG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Valid resonance structures of carbon dioxide

questiontext.text: Identify the correct resonance structures of carbon dioxide from the ones given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)) has \(16\) valence electrons and is represented as a resonance hybrid of Lewis structures that obey the octet rule and carry appropriate formal charges.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the major neutral resonance contributor \(\mathrm{O} = \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{O}\), carbon forms two double bonds with oxygen, giving every atom a complete octet and zero formal charge. In the minor charge-separated contributors with one single bond and one triple bond, the triple-bonded oxygen atom has \(3\) bonding pairs and \(1\) lone pair, giving it a formal charge of \(6 - 2 - 3 = +1\) (\(\equiv \mathrm{O}^+\)), while the single-bonded oxygen atom carries a formal charge of \(-1\). Placing a \(+1\) formal charge on the single-bonded oxygen atom as in \(\mathrm{O}\equiv \mathrm{C} - \mathrm{O}^{+}\) or omitting the positive charge on the triple-bonded oxygen atom as in \(\mathrm{O} - \mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{O}\) violates formal-charge and electron-count rules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The valid resonance structures among those shown are \(\mathrm{O} = \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{O - C}\equiv \mathrm{O}^{+}\).
